snippet.title: Could You Survive Stepping Onto Saturn's Moon Titan?
snippet.description:
What Would Happen If You Landed on Titan? (Seas of Liquid Gas) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T3cBBss1F60

If you stepped out of a lander onto Saturn's largest moon, Titan, would you survive? Your body would not explode, and your blood would not boil. While spacecraft in orbit around Saturn fly through a vacuum, Titan wraps itself in an orange nitrogen sky that presses about 1.5 times harder (1.47 bar) than the air in your room right now. That pressure would not hurt you at all — what would kill you is the deep cold (-179 °C) and the fact that there is almost no oxygen to breathe.

Sources: Fulchignoni et al. (2005), Nature — Huygens surface pressure (1,467 hPa / 1.47 bar) and temperature (93.65 K / -179.5 °C) measurements (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04314); Lebreton et al. (2005), Nature — Huygens descent and landing on Titan (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04347); NASA Science, Titan Facts — dense nitrogen-rich atmosphere and surface conditions (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/titan/facts/).

Image credits: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Goddard Space Flight Center/Steve Gribben (Dragonfly SVS 20311 animations and surface stills); NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute (Cassini ISS: PIA12621, PIA14922, PIA20016, PIA22766); NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/University of Idaho/DLR (Cassini VIMS: PIA21434); NASA Johnson Space Center (Apollo 17 AS17-148-22727); NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, J. DePasquale (STScI) (JWST NIRCam weic2310a, CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

Pictures: Original animated explainers alongside NASA/ESA/CSA/APL imagery, with AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
